questions.prompt: Range [0,2] metres, 200 bins: worst-case reconstruction error in millimetres? (2 decimals)
Bin index for a=-0.25 in range [-1,1] with 8 bins?
Centre value reconstructed for bin 5 of 8 over [-1,1]? (3 decimals)
A 6-token action decoded at 30 tokens/s; chunks of 3 actions per call. How many model calls per second are needed to execute at 5 actions/s? (1 decimal)
questions.explanation: 5 actions/s / 3 per call = 1.67 calls/s; each call needs 18 tokens = 0.6 s, so decoding fits.

questions.prompt: Wilson 95% interval, 16/20 successes: UPPER bound? (2 decimals)
Wilson 95% interval for 0 successes in 20 trials: UPPER bound? (3 decimals)
Seen-object success is 36/40 and held-out-object success is 24/40, each in different scenes. Why is it unsafe to blame language grounding?
options: Wilson intervals do not apply to ratios of successes, so the gap has no uncertainty.
Forty trials is always enough, so the gap is certainly caused by language grounding.
Held-out objects cannot be tested in a scene, so any comparison with them is invalid.
Scene difficulty changed with the objects, so object novelty is confounded with scene.
questions.explanation: A fair comparison keeps the scene fixed.

questions.prompt: Instruction sensitivity is 0.0 for three conflicting instructions on the same observation. What does it show?
options: The tokenizer is broken and drops the instruction text
The policy is perfectly accurate on all three instructions
The policy ignores the instruction in that scene.
The three instructions are in fact paraphrases of one
questions.explanation: Identical actions for different targets indicate no use of language.

questions.prompt: Which is a counterfactual test for language use?
options: Keep the image identical and change 'red cube' to 'blue ball'.
Change both the image and the instruction at once.
Train a second model with different seeds.

questions.prompt: Four instructions are given on the same observation, which makes 6 unordered instruction pairs. The policy outputs different actions for 3 of the 6 pairs. What is the instruction sensitivity (fraction of pairs with different actions)?
A VLA trained on 100 scenes scores 85% on those scenes and 82% on 20 new scenes with the same objects. Which is the most defensible reading?
options: Little evidence of a scene gap, but object and instruction generalisation remain untested.
The VLA generalises to all novel conditions, including new objects and new instructions.
The VLA memorised the training scenes, since 82% is below the 85% training score.
Twenty held-out scenes are too few to compute any success rate or interval.
questions.explanation: Each axis needs its own test.

questions.prompt: Write a short evaluation plan comparing a VLA to a scripted baseline on held-out objects, including trials per condition, confidence intervals, and failure categories.
rubric: Equal trials, same scenes, randomised order and intervals (e.g. Wilson).
Failures categorised (perception, wrong object, grasp, language) rather than only a rate.
A scripted or oracle baseline for task difficulty and a falsifier set in advance.
